name: Laddering

card.summary: Stepping up the strength or frequency of a retinoid in stages so skin adapts, aiming for smoother, clearer-looking skin at a higher strength.
card.note: Retinoids can cause dryness, redness and flaking, and increased sun sensitivity; they are not recommended in pregnancy.

quick.overview:
Laddering (retinol laddering) is a way of introducing a retinoid in steps: starting with low frequency or a low-strength product, and moving up one level at a time as skin tolerates it. People use it to reach stronger retinoid products, which are associated with improvements in fine lines, rough texture and tone, while keeping irritation manageable.

Skincare brands and dermatologists describe the approach as 'slow and steady.' Clinical sources on tretinoin note that improvement in photoaging typically takes several weeks or months of use.
quick.how: Commonly described schedules begin with application on a couple of nights a week, move to every other night and then nightly, hold at one strength for around six weeks or longer, and only then step to the next strength, repeating the phase-in. Moisturiser, a gentle cleanser and daily sunscreen are typically paired with it.
quick.risks: The common effect is retinoid dermatitis: redness, flaking, dryness and itching, usually managed by reducing frequency. Skin can be more sun-sensitive. Retinoids have additional restrictions in pregnancy; product labelling and clinicians give individual guidance.

lead: Laddering is the practice of climbing a retinoid 'ladder' in small steps, raising frequency first and then strength, rather than starting at a high strength. The aim is to reach the higher-strength products that skincare users associate with a smoother, more even complexion while giving skin time to adapt.

Brands such as Medik8 publish step-up guides: use the current product for at least six weeks, ideally finishing a tube, and, if results are good, stay at the current strength for two to three months before moving up. Their schedule phases a product in at twice a week for two weeks, every other night for two weeks, then nightly if there is no irritation, repeating the process at each new strength [1]. The brand calls the transient dryness during an increase 'retinization' [1].

Medical references describe the same logic for tretinoin: if irritation is a problem, apply every other or every third night and raise frequency as tolerance improves [2]. Topical tretinoin, the most studied retinoid for photoaging, increases collagen production and typically needs weeks to months before improvement is seen [2].

chain: Start at low frequency or strength
Step up to a stronger product
angle.text: Retinoids are used for fine lines, texture and tone. Laddering is the tolerance-building routine that lets people use them consistently at a stronger level, since consistent use is what produces visible change.

infobox: Retinol, retinal, tretinoin and other retinoids

paras: Retinoids are derivatives of vitamin A. Retinol is an over-the-counter form; tretinoin is the prescription acid form. The most common side effect of topical retinoids is retinoid dermatitis, with redness, flaking, dryness and itching [3]. Laddering responds to this by changing one variable at a time, frequency or strength.

The Medik8 guide says readiness to step up includes at least six weeks of use, no dryness, flaking, burning or redness, and results that have plateaued; if irritation occurs after an increase, it advises reducing frequency, letting skin settle and repeating the cycle [1]. Dermatologists quoted in consumer guidance give differing time frames, so week counts vary by source.

Increased sun sensitivity is thought to result from thinning of the stratum corneum and irritation; the tretinoin literature notes that topical retinoids are not true photosensitizers [2]. Brand guidance advises daily sunscreen because of increased cell turnover [1].
In the EU and UK, retinol in cosmetics is capped at 0.3 percent for most leave-on and rinse-off products and 0.05 percent for body lotion, with labelling required [3].

No studies found testing laddering schedules as such. Studies of tretinoin for photoaging have run for up to two years, and lower-concentration or less frequent maintenance regimens are described as an option [2]. Studies have examined retinol's effect on fine wrinkles and rough texture, with improvement not persisting after use stops [3].

timeline.event: Tretinoin approved for medical use; FDA approval for acne followed in 1971 [2].
